doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Outings with the welfare hotel children
summary: She describes the crackdown on welfare hotels, taking children to ballet and opera, and their request to see Halloween 4.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So by now you’ve moved from just south of the George Washington Bridge to the upper West Side across the river.
Where was the welfare hotel that you...
Where a lot of them were at that time. We’re talking about the late ’80s now?
Is what you’re referring to the organization Children Of Substance?
This is what leads up to that.

This leads up to that. Then the welfare hotels...the city cracked down and realized it was all some kind of contracting underground nightmare, and there were payoffs going on all over the place. Because the city was giving these welfare hotel owners $2000 a month per room for people to live without cooking facilities, without your own bathroom. Kids would have to go to the front desk and ask for three...they’d have to ask for toilet paper to use the bathroom. How demeaning. I mean, that was the motivating factor in why I wanted to do this, because I wanted them to see another side of life, that this was not all you are being offered, that “the world is a lot bigger than this and this is not what I want you to expect out of life.” So we’d take them to the opera, to the ballet. Peter Martins at New York City Ballet gave us free tickets to Nutcracker, and the girls, the ballerinas would meet them before the show, and give them toe-shows. Even the boys would put the toe-shoes on. It was a moving experience. I remember once asking them what did they want to do. I said, ‘I know...” Oh, that’s what it is. They came to me and they said, “I know we’re always doing this opera stuff and this ballet stuff, but could we do stuff, like, that we really want to do.” I was like, “Sure, what would that be?” They wanted to go see, like, Halloween 4. So I had to go take them to see...which I am completely unable to see things like that. I’m a true empath. I feel everything I see or hear. I can’t watch the news for that reason. I had my feet up on the seat and my eyes closed the whole time, and they thought it was hysterical. We had the best time.
These things didn’t just happen by themselves. They happened because people, probably you, were pitching people to contribute...
